criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community access to water supply and sanitation services (WSS) in Brazil, with particular attention to deficits in rural and informal peri-urban areas.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: Yes — examines legal, institutional, regulatory, and governance frameworks in the Brazilian water and sanitation sector (including Federal Laws no. 11.445/2007 and no. 14.026/2020, ministries, and subnational regulators). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Yes (borderline with macro-governance) — although the overarching thesis concerns macro-level alignment of policies, institutions, and regulation (isomorphic mimicry), the paper also discusses rule-type utility ownership, concession contracting, and regulatory jurisdiction rules governing access, such as the exclusion of informal peri-urban and rural areas from regulatory agency mandates and contracts. Under both the plain and narrow readings of Criterion 2, the overall screening decision remains exclude because the paper fails Criterion 3 (E05, no empirical evidence).
criterion_notes.c3: No empirical evidence or systematic empirical synthesis. Although the authors refer to Brazil as a case study, the article has no methods or data section, collects no primary data, conducts no quantitative or qualitative empirical analysis, and follows no systematic review protocol; it is a narrative policy, legal, and institutional overview and conceptual commentary citing secondary literature and official headline statistics.
criterion_notes.c4: Cites secondary official national statistics on water supply and wastewater collection coverage deficits in Brazil (e.g., MDR 2019; IBGE 2020), though no empirical outcome analysis is conducted.
criterion_notes.c5: No identifiable empirical study design, empirical sample, or empirical analytical framework linking an exposure to an outcome; the text is a narrative sector-level commentary.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in English, an eligible language without translation.

evidence_quotes.quote: This article discusses the barriers to WSS universal access in Brazil. By analyzing policies, institutions, and regulation (PIR) and the associated enabling environment, we assert that the leading cause of failure is isomorphic mimicry.
In this document, access to WSS in Brazil is analyzed as a case study. We discuss different public policies, institutions, and regulation (PIR) in the country, with a focus on vulnerable areas.

In the third section, the central public policies for WSS in Brazil are presented and discussed. Next, the WSS institutional framework is described and analyzed, and section five shows how WSS sector regulation in the country have been carried out.
In 2018, approximately 16% of the country’s population did not have access to a sustainable water supply service, and 47% did not have wastewater collection services (MDR, 2019).

Even more restrictive is that, with very few exceptions, regulatory agencies do not include the regulation of vulnerable areas (peri-urban and rural areas). In the areas where there is a greater need for regulation, it does not exist.

raw_response.exposure: Brazilian water and sanitation policies, institutions, and regulation (PIR), including Law no. 11.445/2007, Law no. 14.026/2020, municipal/concession ownership rules, and decentralized regulatory governance
raw_response.outcome: Universal access / service coverage for water supply and wastewater collection (secondary national statistics cited descriptively only)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Brazilian water and sanitation sector at the national level, highlighting vulnerable rural and informal peri-urban populations (no empirical sample)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). While the paper discusses water and sanitation service access in Brazil and examines legal, institutional, and regulatory structures (including Law no. 11.445/2007, Law no. 14.026/2020, decentralized subnational regulators, and the exclusion of rural and informal peri-urban areas from regulation), it is a narrative policy/institutional overview and conceptual essay arguing that reforms suffer from isomorphic mimicry. It presents no empirical research design, no primary qualitative or quantitative data, no empirical analysis of secondary micro/panel data, and no systematic review methodology.
raw_response.study_design: Narrative policy and institutional overview / conceptual commentary (non-empirical)
